cards.title: Budget existing-customer retargeting by dollar and frequency, not percent
cards.summary: Replace 'existing customer spend percentage' with a dollar budget derived from customer count, CPM, and desired monthly frequency, judged on profit and frequency.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing retargeting/existing-customer budget allocation in your Meta ad account for a store with a growing customer list.
steps: Recognize why percentage-of-spend is misleading: the same percent means very different absolute reach depending on how big your existing-customer pool is and how much you're spending on new-customer acquisition, so the number shifts without any real change in strategy.

Instead answer two questions: (1) Is existing-customer spend profitable — if you add another $10 or $1,000/day, does the incremental revenue cover the spend and produce profit? (2) What is the frequency on existing customers — high frequency (the source gives the extreme example of 50 impressions per customer per 30 days) signals over-spend, frequency of ~1 suggests under-spend.

Calculate a monthly dollar budget: number of existing customers × CPM × desired frequency per month. Example logic: if you have 50,000 customers, your CPM is $10, and you want 2 impressions per customer per month, the monthly budget is roughly 50,000 × 0.01 × 2 = $1,000.
Set the budget in dollars rather than filling in a percentage cap field, and re-derive it when the customer count or CPM changes.
Review frequency alongside profitability each period rather than trusting the spend-percentage number.
caveats: The formula is the source's heuristic; your CPM and desired frequency are inputs you must supply from your own account and margin, not fixed benchmarks.
The source's frequency-50 example is an illustration of over-targeting, not a threshold that applies universally.

cards.title: Avoiding the DPA death spiral: protect top-of-funnel investment
cards.summary: Shifting budget from top-of-funnel prospecting into DPAs lifts DPA-reported revenue short-term but starves the funnel and causes account-wide decline; keep top-of-funnel spend and creative throughput protected.
cards.use_when: When DPA/retargeting ROAS looks strong and you're tempted to raise its budget, cut prospecting, or reduce creative production.
steps: Understand the mechanism: DPAs sit at the bottom of the funnel and capture revenue generated by top-of-funnel demand. Increase top-of-funnel budget and DPA reported revenue rises; cut top-of-funnel and DPA performance eventually falls — the source calls this the 'DPA death spiral'.

Watch for the pattern the source observed across six fashion-brand audits: ~80% of spend on DPAs, good reported DPA performance, budgets repeatedly increased, then declining account performance over ~6 months.

Do not let strong DPA ROAS justify reducing creative production or top-of-funnel allocation — the source reports agencies advised brands they didn't need as much creative because DPAs were 'holding up'; the business subsequently fell apart.
When DPA performance softens, check top-of-funnel spend and creative output before cutting or reallocating further — the fix is usually upstream, not in the DPA layer.
Treat DPA/retargeting as a support layer sized to actual retention and new-customer inflow, not as the primary growth engine.
caveats: The six-brand pattern is a case observation from the source's audits, not a measured benchmark across all accounts.
Some bottom-funnel capture effect is normal; the warning is about starving top-of-funnel and creative throughput, not about running DPAs at all.

cards.title: Turn off Meta flexible ads to preserve creative read-outs
cards.summary: Flexible ads bundle multiple assets into one ad with no visibility into which creative drove results, breaking your data feedback loop; only use them with near-identical assets.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad formats when launching Meta creative tests or trying to work around the account's ad/page limits.
steps: Skip flexible ads as a default because you can't tell which asset drove performance when the ad wins or loses, which violates the data-integrity foundation needed for decision-making.

Only consider flexible ads if you're forced to by page limits and you've exhausted better workarounds (splitting across pages/accounts); in that case load only very similar creative so a positive result still tells you 'this type of ad works'.
Never mix large variation in asset types inside one flexible ad — you lose the ability to read results and add non-decision-useful data to the account.
Account for presentation risks: you don't control cropping, 1:1 and story assets may be served into feed placements, and Meta may string flexible ads into an unapproved carousel of random images.
If an unapproved carousel or bad crop is a client or brand risk, keep creative in standard ad types with controlled placements.
caveats: The source's agency 'really doesn't like flexible ads'; this is a strong situational opinion favoring data integrity over the convenience of consolidating assets.
If page limits genuinely force consolidation, flexible ads with similar creative are the fallback rather than an outright ban.

cards.title: Deprioritize cost caps and bid caps below ~$200k/month
cards.summary: Bidding strategy is low-leverage for most sub-$200k/month ad accounts; solve other bottlenecks first and treat cost caps as an advanced lever, not a growth switch.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to spend time testing cost caps or bid caps in a Meta ad account, or when someone proposes bidding changes as the growth plan.
steps: Apply the source's test: ask whether the business would double if you focused entirely on bidding strategies in Meta — the source says the answer is normally no, making it low leverage.
If the account is spending under about $200,000/month, prioritize other bottlenecks (structure, creative throughput, offer, funnel allocation) before bidding strategy changes.
If you do understand cost caps well, the source acknowledges you can run them at any spend level — so this is about where to focus effort, not a prohibition.

When bidding strategy is raised as the fix, quantify the expected upside against alternative levers (more creative concepts, better top-of-funnel allocation, structure changes) before committing test budget.
Revisit bidding strategy once the account is at a spend tier where the source considers it material.
caveats: The ~$200k/month figure is the source's stated heuristic threshold, not a measured law.
The source explicitly says experienced operators can run cost caps at any spend level; this is a priority judgment, not a capability limit.

cards.title: Disable 1-day view attribution for budget and scaling decisions
cards.summary: One-day-view attribution over-attributes revenue, especially from existing customers, so exclude it from adset budget-flow and scaling decisions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Meta reporting to decide which adsets to scale, cut, or shift budget between.
steps: Turn off one-day view attribution, or at minimum exclude it from the decision process for flowing budget at adset level and judging what's working.

Understand the distortion: 1-day view substantially over-attributes conversions to existing-customer revenue, which can make existing-customer and retargeting adsets look more productive than they are.
Choose a consistent attribution window and apply it uniformly when comparing prospecting vs. existing-customer adsets.
When an adset's performance looks strong only on 1-day view, verify the result on a longer, click-based window before increasing its budget.
caveats: The source's objection is specifically about using 1-day view for budget decisions; it does not claim the metric has zero value for all purposes.
Attribution windows and settings in Meta change over time — verify the current interface when configuring.

cards.title: Turn off Advantage+ creative optimizations at account and ad level
cards.summary: Advantage+ creative optimizations re-enable themselves over time unless you disable them in advertiser settings, so turn them off at both account and individual ad level to keep creative testing clean.
cards.use_when: Auditing Meta ad account setup before launching creative tests, or when creative settings keep reverting unexpectedly.
steps: Turn off automated creative optimization settings on every ad you launch — the source notes this is tedious but necessary.

Also disable them in advertiser settings (navigate to the creative sub-dropdown, which contains automated rules). If you only turn them off per-ad, the account-level rules will flip creative optimization back on over time.
After disabling, spot-check recently launched ads to confirm the settings held, since account-level rules can silently re-enable them.
Treat these automatic optimizations as a threat to data integrity: if Meta is auto-modifying creative, you can't cleanly attribute performance to the asset you intended to test.
caveats: Menu labels and locations inside Meta Ads Manager change frequently — verify the current path to advertiser settings and the creative sub-dropdown before instructing your team.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Audit audience segment syncs to prevent existing customers being served as new
cards.summary: Broken audience-segment syncs (e.g. Klaviyo to Meta) cause existing customers to be targeted as new, eroding data integrity and wasting spend.
cards.use_when: Routine ad-account audits or when existing-customer/new-customer reporting looks inconsistent with your CRM or email platform.
steps: Set up your existing-customer audience segments (commonly synced from a platform like Klaviyo to Meta) and verify the sync is active.

Periodically check that the sync hasn't silently broken — the source reports these syncs break periodically, and when they do, existing customers stop flowing into the existing-customer exclusion/segment.
When the sync is broken, you end up spending on existing customers while treating them as new, which erodes data integrity and puts budget in places you don't want.
Make segment-sync verification a recurring audit step alongside creative and structure checks, not a one-time setup task.
If you see new-customer metrics degrading without an obvious creative or offer cause, check segment sync before changing bids or budgets.
caveats: Specific connector behavior (Klaviyo to Meta) and interface steps may change; verify current integration setup and sync status in the actual tools.

cards.title: Size test budgets from target conversions, CPA, and duration
cards.summary: Calculate a test's daily budget as (target conversions × expected CPA) ÷ test duration in days, choosing the conversion threshold and learning speed explicitly before launch.
cards.use_when: Planning any Meta ad test (creative concept, audience, structure) and needing to know how much to spend and for how long.
steps: Answer two questions before launch: what conversion count is your statistical-significance threshold (e.g. 5, 10, 20), and over how many days do you want to learn (3, 7, 14, 30)?
Compute daily test budget = (target conversions × expected CPA) ÷ test duration in days. Example from the source: 20 target conversions × $100 CPA ÷ 14 days = ~$143/day.

Compare against Meta's standard advice of 50 conversions per 7 days: at $100 CPA that requires $714/day for a single concept adset, which the source calls unrealistic for most advertisers once you run several tests.
Because Meta's 50/7 guidance blows out test budgets, use your own commercially viable threshold instead of defaulting to platform guidance.
Decide up front what result ends the test and what action (scale, kill, or extend) follows at the threshold.
caveats: The 20-conversion, $100-CPA, 14-day example is the source's worked illustration, not a benchmark; your threshold depends on your traffic, margin, and risk tolerance.
Meta's learning-phase guidance and definitions change over time — verify the current platform documentation.

cards.title: Four-question checklist to validate any ad account structure
cards.summary: Judge account structure by whether it produces readable data, matches how the business makes profit, fits your spend/creative tier, and sizes support layers to actual retention.
cards.use_when: Designing a new Meta account structure or auditing an existing one, especially after scaling spend or changing creative output.
steps: Question 1 — Data readability: does the structure produce data you can read to make decisions? The source calls this the whole point of account structure: readable data enables continued iteration.
Question 2 — Commercial alignment: does the structure match how the business actually makes money? Structure should reflect how profit is produced, not an abstract ideal.

Question 3 — Spend-tier fit: is the structure appropriate for your spend level and creative throughput? The amount you spend and how much creative you can produce substantially change what structure is workable.

Question 4 — Support layers: are DPA, retargeting, website visitors, and existing-customer layers aligned with actual retention? Determine how much spend these layers need based on real retention, not a fixed percentage.
If any answer is no, restructure rather than patching — the source treats any 'no' as a signal the structure is wrong.
caveats: This is a qualitative checklist, not a scoring system; 'appropriate for spend tier' is context-dependent and the source gives no fixed spend thresholds for structure types.
Answers depend on business specifics — margins, retention, creative capacity — so conclusions differ by store.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Review the whole ad account at once when auditing spend allocation
cards.summary: Don't evaluate one adset or campaign in isolation; audit spend allocation across all campaigns and support layers to spot problems like top-of-funnel starvation or DPA over-weighting.
cards.use_when: Running an audit of a store's Meta ad account, or diagnosing declining account performance when individual campaigns look fine.
steps: Audit the entire account in one review rather than stopping at the campaign with the best or worst performance — the source's DPA death-spiral finding came from seeing patterns across full audits of six brands, not single campaigns.
Check the distribution of spend across top-of-funnel prospecting, DPA, retargeting, and existing-customer layers together, since each layer's reported performance is affected by the others.
Look for allocation drift over several months (the source's example: accounts at ~80% DPA spend with declining performance over ~6 months), rather than reacting only to this week's numbers.
Trace declines back through related decisions — creative production volume, top-of-funnel budget cuts, agency advice — rather than assuming an isolated campaign underperforms.
Use your four-question structure checklist to test whether the current allocation still matches how the business makes money.
caveats: The six-brand observation is a pattern the source noticed in a specific audit window, not a controlled study.
Spend distribution is context-dependent on retention and business model, per the source's own framing.
